questions.q: I am registered to vote in Shawnee, but I work in Oklahoma City. Can I vote in Oklahoma City?
questions.a: No. State law requires that you register to vote according to your address of residence. You may vote only at the polling place to which you are assigned based on the address where you are registered. (But you can request an absentee ballot (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/absentee-voting.html) or vote early (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/early-voting.html).)

questions.q: I am registered to vote in Tulsa, but I am in college in Norman. Can I vote in Norman?
questions.a:
You can request to have an absentee ballot (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/absentee-voting.html) mailed to you in Norman or you may choose to register to vote in Norman. If you register in Norman, your registration in Tulsa will be canceled.

questions.q: What is an Address Confirmation Notice?
questions.a:
An Address Confirmation Notice is a mailing sent to select voters by the State Election Board every two years, as part of the statutorily-mandated, voter list maintenance process required by law.

Voters are selected to receive an Address Confirmation Notice for one of several reasons as outlined in 26 O.S. § 4-120.2 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=78475). Voters who receive the notice must respond and confirm their registration address. Voters who do not respond will have their status changed to “inactive.”

“Inactive” voters who do not vote and have no further voter activity, such as updating their address or party affiliation, are required to be removed from the voter list following two, consecutive general elections for Federal office.

View a sample of the Address Confirmation Notice. (https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/elections/address-confirmation-notices/2025-address-confirmation-notice.pdf)

questions.q: Why did I get an Address Confirmation Notice?
questions.a: Voters may receive an Address Confirmation Notice for one of several reasons as outlined in 26 O.S. § 4-120.2 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=78475). You will find additional information on our Address Confirmation Notice (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/address-confirmation-notice.html) page. If you would like to know the specific reason you received a notice, please contact your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html).

questions.q: I received an Address Confirmation notice, but my spouse did not. Why?
questions.a: Not every voter will receive an Address Confirmation Notice. The reasons a voter may receive an Address Confirmation Notice are specified by law. You will find the list of reasons outlined in 26 O.S. § 4-120.2 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=78475). Additional information is available on our Address Confirmation Notice (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/address-confirmation-notice.html) page. If you would like more information regarding why you received a notice, please contact your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html).

questions.q: Why does the return card have a different P.O. Box address than the one listed on the State Election Board website?
questions.a: The State Election Board has a special P.O. Box to receive the Address Confirmation Notice return cards.

questions.q: Can I return the card to my County Election Board in person?
questions.a: Yes. Find your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html).

questions.q: Can the card be returned inside an envelope?
questions.a: Yes. However, the return card is designed to be folded, so that all personal information is inside. Please see our Address Confirmation Notice (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/address-confirmation-notice.html) page for return instructions.

questions.q: Can I verify my address over the phone or online?
questions.a: You cannot verify your address over the phone; however, you can verify your address online using the OK Voter Portal (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/). You will need the 8-digit number printed above your name and address on the Address Confirmation Notice to confirm your information online.

questions.q: Will every voter in the state get a notice?
questions.a: No. Only voters that meet the criteria in 26 O.S. § 4-120.2 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=78475) will receive a notice.

questions.q: I still live at the same address, but my name has changed. Can I use this card to change my name?
questions.a:
Yes. If you have not already submitted a new Voter Registration Application to change your name, the return card can be used for this purpose.

Complete the card providing your "current name" and "previous name." Be sure to sign and date the Address Confirmation Notice Return Card before mailing it. Your registration will be updated to indicate your new name and you will receive a new Voter ID card by mail.

questions.q: I received an Address Confirmation Notice, but have moved to another state. Do I still need to respond?
questions.a:
Yes. Fill out the card, including your "current residence address" and "current mailing address." Be sure to check the box that says, "I no longer reside in the State of Oklahoma. Please cancel my Oklahoma voter registration." Sign and date the card and mail it.

County Election Board personnel in your former county can use the signed, Return Card to cancel your voter registration in Oklahoma. If you don’t return the card, your registration will become “inactive” and will not be cancelled for several years.

questions.q: What happens if I do not return the notice to the Election Board?
questions.a:
By law, a voter’s registration will become “inactive” if the notice is not returned within 60 days. The law requires the Election Board to cancel the voter registration of an “inactive voter” who (1) does not initiate a voter registration change, or (2) does not vote in any election conducted by a county election board during the designated time period, following the mailing date of an Address Confirmation Notice.

The designated period of time is defined as “two, consecutive general elections for Federal office.”

If your voter registration statuts becomes "inactive," you may still vote; however, you will be asked to update your voter registration when you cast your ballot at your polling place or early voting location. Voting and/or updating your registration will automatically reverse your "inactive" status to "active."

questions.q: The addressee is now in a nursing home. Should the card be returned?
questions.a:
If the voter wants to remain registered, the voter’s spouse or child should take the Address Confirmation Notice to the nursing home, have the voter sign it and mail it. If the voter does not want to remain registered, the voter should complete a Request to Cancel Voter Registration (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voter-registration/cancel-voter-registration.html) form and return it to their County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html). If the voter does not respond, the voter’s registration will be cancelled following two, consecutive general elections for Federal office.

IMPORTANT: There is no provision in state law to allow a voter’s next-of-kin to cancel a voter registration if the voter is still living.

questions.q: The addressee no longer lives at this location. What should I do?
questions.a: If you know the voter’s address, you can forward the card to the voter. If you do not know the voter's address - write “not at this address" on the front of the mailpiece and place the card back in your mailbox to be returned to the County Election Board.

questions.q: The addressee is deceased. Should the card be returned?
questions.a: No. The deceased voter’s next-of-kin should submit a Request to Cancel Voter Registration of Deceased Voter (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voter-registration/cancel-voter-registration.html) form to the voter’s former County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html).

questions.q: My voter registration was deleted. Can I register again?
questions.a: Yes. If you have been removed from the voter rolls, you may register again by completing a new Voter Registration Application (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) using the OK Voter Portal's Online Voter Registration System. Voter Registration Applications are also available at your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html), most tag agencies, libraries, and post offices.

questions.q: How do I keep my registration from being deleted?
questions.a:
Respond to any Address Confirmation Notice you receive and keep your registration current. You can keep your registration current by voting or updating your registration if you move or change your name using the OK Voter Portal (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/ovp.html).

If you move to another county in Oklahoma, you will need to submit a new Voter Registration Application (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voter-registration/voter-registration-changes.html). Be sure to include your prior address in the spaces provided on the form.

questions.q: I didn’t get a notice, but believe I may need to update my registration. Is there a way to verify my voter information?
questions.a:
You can verify your voter registration information and make changes to your registration using the OK Voter Portal (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/ovp.html). If you have moved to a new county or changed your name, you will need to submit a new Voter Registration Application (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voter-registration/voter-registration-changes.html) to your new County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html).

1. I have received a State of Oklahoma Voter Address Confirmation card in the mail. Is it really from the State Election Board?

Address confirmation forms are sent to some registered voters to help us verify and update voter registration records. Federal and state laws require us to send these cards every two years. This document (https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/elections/address-confirmation-notices/address-confirmation-2019/2019%20%20Confirmation%20Notice%20Card.pdf) is an example of what the mailing looks like.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

2. Why does the Return Card have a different P. O. Box address than the one listed on the State Election Board website?

The State Election Board has a special P. O. Box to receive the Address Confirmation Notice Return Cards.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

3. Can I return the card to my County Election Board in person?

Yes.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

4. Can the card be returned inside an envelope?

Yes. However, the return card is designed to be folded and sealed with tape so that all personal information is inside.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

5. Can I verify my address over the phone or online?

You cannot verify your address over the phone. However, you can verify your address by using our Online Voter Tool (https://services.okelections.us/voterSearch.aspx). Enter your information into the search, and when the page with your voter registration opens, look for the "Voter Confirmation" section. Enter the 8-digit number above your name and address on the mailing, and then follow the on-screen instructions. The law requires the voter return the card by regular mail, deliver it in person to the voter's County Election Board office or verify their address online using the Online Voter Tool.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

6. Why did I get this notice?

Federal and state laws require us to confirm voters' addresses periodically.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

7. Will every voter in the state get a notice?

No. Only some voters will receive a notice. Some family members may receive a card while others may not. Those who do not receive a card are not in danger of being removed from the voter registration rolls.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

8. Which voters will get a notice?

Voters who fall into one of five categories will receive a notice. The categories are:

- Voter has not voted since before the 2016 General Election.
- Voter has the same last name, first initial, and birth date as another voter in the state.
- First-class mailing sent to voter since January 1, 2017, was returned by the post office as undeliverable.
- Voter surrendered Oklahoma driver license in another state.
- Voter may have registered to vote in another state.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

9. The addressee is deceased. Should the card be returned?

No. The card should be thrown away. If you are a member of the deceased voter's family, you may submit a form (https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/elections/forms/Request%20To%20Cancel%20Registration%20Of%20Deceased%20Voter.pdf) to the County Election Board to cancel the voter's registration. This form either must be notarized or witnessed by two people who include their names and addresses on the form.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

10. The addressee is now in a nursing home. Should the card be returned?

If the voter wants to remain registered, the voter's spouse or child should take the confirmation card to the nursing home, have the voter sign it, and then mail it. If the voter does not want to remain registered, the card should be thrown away. The voter's registration will be canceled following the 2022 General Election. (The voter may submit a notarized cancellation request (https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/elections/forms/vr_cancel.pdf) in order to be canceled sooner.) There is no provision in state law to allow a voter's next-of-kin to cancel voter registration if the voter is still living.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

11. I still live at the same address, but my name has changed. Can I use this card to change my name?

Yes. If you have not already submitted a new voter registration application to change your name, the return card can be used for this purpose. Complete the card, indicating your new last name. In the margin just above the name, write "name has changed due." Your registration record will be updated to indicate your new name, and you will receive a new voter identification card.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

12. I have moved within the county and my name has changed. Can I use the card to change both my name and address?

Yes. If you have not already submitted a new voter registration application to change your name and address within the county, you can use the return card for this purpose. Complete the card, indicating your new last name. In the margin just above the name, write "name has changed." List the new address. Your record will be updated to indicate your new name and address, and you will receive a new voter identification card.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

13. The voter is no longer at this location. What should be done?

If you know the voter's new address, write "Moved to: (address)" and return the card. If you do not know the voter's new address, throw the card away.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

14. The voter is away from home (i.e., military voter stationed overseas; voter who works away from home) and will not be home within 60 days. What should be done with the notice?

If you are the spouse or parent of the voter, you may choose to do any of the following:

- Put the notice in an envelope, affix postage, and mail it to the voter.
- Save the confirmation notice until the voter returns home. The voter's registration will become inactive if the notice is not returned within 60 days; however, if the card is returned after the 60-day deadline, but before cancellation following the 2022 General Election, the voter's registration will be reactivated.
- Throw the card away. The voter will become inactive but will be reactivated if he or she votes in any election up to and including the 2022 General Election.

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

15. What happens if I do not return the notice to the Election Board?

By law, a voter's registration will become inactive if the notice is not returned within 60 days. The law requires the Election Board to cancel the voter registration of an inactive voter who (1) does not initiate a voter registration change or (2) does not vote in an election conducted by a county election board by the date of the second General Election for federal office following the date of the confirmation mailing. (For a voter who does not respond to the address confirmation notice in 2019, the voter's registration is required by law to be canceled following the 2022 General Election unless the voter reactivates the voter registration by voting or by initiating a voter registration change.)

Top of Address Confirmation (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c235)

questions.q: Can I vote early?
questions.a:
Yes! You can vote in the county where you are registered to vote from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Thursday and Friday before all elections.

In addition to early voting the Thursday and Friday preceding an election, early voting is also available from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. on the Saturday immediately preceding a State or Federal Primary Election, State or Federal Runoff Primary Election, General Election or Presidential Preferential Primary Election.

Early voting is also available from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. the Wednesday preceding the General Election.

In most counties early voting is held at the county election board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html) office. However, some counties may have an alternate or additional early voting location (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/early-voting.html).

 1. Can I vote early? (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#q621)

1. Can I vote early?

Yes! You can vote at the County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/elections/ceb-physical-addresses/cebinfo1.pdf) office in the county where you are registered to vote from 8 AM to 6 PM on Thursday and Friday before all elections. For state and federal elections only, you also can vote from 9 AM until 2 PM on Saturday before the election. Details (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/early-voting.html).

Top of Early Voting (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c97)

questions.q: Where can I find information about voter registration and absentee voting for military and overseas voters?
questions.a: Military voters should contact the Voting Assistance Officers in their units for application forms and information. Overseas voters may obtain the same materials at United States military installations, embassies and consulates, or online from the Federal Voting Assistance Program. (http://www.fvap.gov/) (You will be redirected to an external site.) Information is available on the State Election Board website (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/military-overseas-voters.html). Military and overseas voters may also contact their County Election Board (https://www.fvap.gov/search-offices?state=36) directly.

questions.q: I am a uniformed services voter. How can I find out whether the County Election Board received my absentee ballot?
questions.a:
An absentee voter who is in the uniformed services or who is a civilian living or working overseas may contact the appropriate County Election Board (https://www.fvap.gov/search-offices?state=36) by email or check the OK Voter Portal (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/ovp.html) for confirmation that the absentee ballot has been received by that election board.

questions.q: I am a Democrat. Can I vote in another party's primary or runoff primary?
questions.a: No. Oklahoma is a closed primary state. Registered voters of a political party may only vote to select their party's nominees.

questions.q: Why do I have to show proof of identity?
questions.a: State law requires all registered voters to show proof of identity before voting in person at the precinct polling place on Election Day or during early voting.

questions.q: What can I show for proof of identity?
questions.a:
You may show any document issued by the United States, the State of Oklahoma, or a federally recognized tribal government if it includes your name, a photograph of you, and an expiration date that is later than the election in which you are voting. For example, the following documents meet these requirements:

- Oklahoma driver license
- Oklahoma Identification Card
- United States passport
- United States military identification

The law also requires that your name on your proof of identity must match your name in the Precinct Registry

There are two alternatives to showing a photo identification described above:

1. You may show the free Voter Identification Card issued by the County Election Board as proof of identity even though it does not include a photograph.

2. You may vote by provisional ballot and prove your identity by signing a sworn affidavit.

questions.q: May I use my tribal membership card as proof of identity?
questions.a: You may use a tribal membership card if it includes your name and a photograph of you, provided it is not expired.

questions.q: What if I do not have proof of identity with me when I go to vote?
questions.a: If you do not show proof of identity, you may vote only by provisional ballot. Voters who cast provisional ballots are required to fill out and sign an affidavit that explains why their provisional ballot should be counted. Provisional ballots are sealed inside special envelopes and are not put through the voting device. After election day, but before results are certified, County Election Board officials will research the information provided by the voter on the affidavit. In order for a provisional ballot to be approved for counting, the information on the affidavit must match the information in the voter's registration record.

questions.q: What happens if I refuse to show proof of identity?
questions.a: If you do not show proof of identity, you may vote only by provisional ballot. Voters who cast provisional ballots are required to fill out and sign an affidavit that explains why their provisional ballot should be counted. Provisional ballots are sealed inside special envelopes and are not put through the voting device. After election day, but before results are certified, County Election Board officials will research the information provided by the voter on the affidavit. In order for a provisional ballot to be approved for counting, the information on the affidavit must match the information in the voter's registration record.

questions.q: If I vote by mail absentee ballot, do I have to enclose a copy of my proof of identity with my ballot?
questions.a:
"Standard" absentee ballots (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/absentee-voting/standard-absentee-voters.html) (the most common type of absentee ballot) must be notarized. "Physically incapacitated" absentee ballots (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/absentee-voting/physically-incapacitated-voters-and-caregivers.html) must have the voter's signature witnessed by two people. The law considers the notarization or witnessing sufficient to establish the identity of an absentee voter.

questions.q: 1. Why do I have to show proof of identity?
questions.a:
State law requires all registered voters to prove their identity before voting in person at the precinct polling place on election day or during early voting at the County Election Board. Details (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/proof-of-identity.html)

Top of Proof of Identity for Voting (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c247)

2. What can I show for proof of identity?

You may show any document issued by the United States, the State of Oklahoma, or a federally recognized tribal government if it includes your name, a photograph of you, and an expiration date that is later than the election in which you are voting. For example, the following documents meet these requirements:

- Oklahoma driver license
- Oklahoma Identification Card
- United States passport
- United States military identification

The law also requires that your name on your proof of identity must match your name in the Precinct Registry

There are two alternatives to showing a photo identification described above:

1. You may show the free Voter Identification Card issued by the County Election Board as proof of identity even though it does not include a photograph.

2. You may vote by provisional ballot and prove your identity by signing a sworn affidavit.

Top of Proof of Identity for Voting (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c247)

3. May I use my tribal membership card as proof of identity?

You may use a tribal membership card if it includes your name and a photograph of you, provided it is not expired.

Top of Proof of Identity for Voting (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c247)

4. What if I do not have proof of identity with me when I go to vote?

If you do not show proof of identity, you may vote only by provisional ballot. Voters who cast provisional ballots are required to fill out and sign an affidavit that explains why their provisional ballot should be counted. Provisional ballots are sealed inside special envelopes and are not put through the voting device. After election day, County Election Board officials will investigate the information provided by the voter on the affidavit and either will approve the provisional ballot for counting or will reject it based on the outcome of that investigation. In order for a provisional ballot to be approved for counting, the information on the affidavit must match the information in the voter's registration record.

Top of Proof of Identity for Voting (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c247)

5. What happens if I refuse to show proof of identity?

If you do not have or if you refuse to show proof of identity, you may vote by provisional ballot and prove your identity by submitting a sworn affidavit with the provisional ballot. Provisional ballots are sealed inside special envelopes and are not put through the voting device. After election day, County Election Board officials will investigate the information provided by the voter on the affidavit and either will approve the provisional ballot for counting or will reject it based on the outcome of that investigation. In order for a provisional ballot to be approved for counting, the information on the affidavit must match the information in the voter's registration record.

Top of Proof of Identity for Voting (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c247)

6. If I vote by mail absentee ballot, do I have to enclose a copy of my proof of identity with my ballot?

No. Most voters who vote by absentee ballot either have their signatures on their affidavits notarized or have them witnessed by two people. The law considers the notarization or witnessing sufficient to establish the identity of an absentee voter.

Top of Proof of Identity for Voting (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/faqs.html#c247)

questions.q: My mother/father/son/daughter, etc., has moved to another state, but his or her name is still on the precinct registry at the polling place. How can I have his or her name removed?
questions.a: Only the voter can request that his or her name be removed. The voter may complete a "Request to Cancel Voter Registration" form (https://author-prod.ok.gov/editor.html/content/sok-wcm/en/elections/voter-registration/cancel-voter-registration.html) and send it to the County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html) in the county where he or she is registered, requesting that his or her voter registration be canceled. The request must be signed by the voter and notarized or the voter's signature must be witnessed by two people.

questions.q: My family member is deceased, but his or her name is still on the precinct registry at the polling place. How can I have his or her name removed?
questions.a: The deceased voter's next of kin may complete a "Request to Cancel Registration of Deceased Voter" form at the polling place. The next of kin may also download a request form (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voter-registration/cancel-voter-registration.html) from the State Election Board website and send the request to the County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html) in the county where the deceased voter is registered. The request must be notarized.

questions.q: How can I get a list of registered voters?
questions.a: Voter registration data is available at no cost through the State Election Board's OK Election Data Warehouse (EDW). To obtain access to the EDW and the voter registration list, you must complete and submit a request form, which can be found on our Voter Registration List webpage (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/candidates/voter-registration-list.html).

questions.q: How can I get voters' telephone numbers?
questions.a: A voter's telephone number is neither required nor requested on the Oklahoma Voter Registration Application; therefore, this information is not maintained by the State Election Board.

questions.q: How can I get candidates' telephone numbers and e-mail addresses?
questions.a: Although it is not required, candidates may include telephone numbers, email addresses and/or website addresses on their Declaration of Candidacy. Declarations of Candidacy for county or local candidates can be requested from the appropriate county election board. Declarations of Candidacy for state or federal candidates are available on the State Election Board website through the Candidate Filing Portal (https://filings.okelections.gov/).

questions.q: How can I identify a voter's race/color/gender/ethnic origin, etc.?
questions.a:
Voter registration records do not include any of these types of information.

questions.q: How do I register to vote in Oklahoma?
questions.a: You can register to vote using the OK Voter Portal's Online Voter Registration System (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/ovp.html). Applications are also available at your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html), most tag agencies, post offices, and public libraries. Visit our website (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voter-registration/register-to-vote.html) for more details.

questions.q: How do I change my name, address or political affiliation on my voter registration?
questions.a: You can make changes to your address (provided you have not moved to a new county) or party affiliation online using the OK Voter Portal (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home). If you have moved to a new county, you will need to complete a new Voter Registration Application (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) and mail or hand-deliver the application to your County Election Board. Applications are also available at your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html), most tag agencies, post offices, and public libraries.

questions.q: I lost my Voter ID card. How do I get a replacement?
questions.a:
You can request a replacement Voter ID card using the OK Voter Portal (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/ovp.html), by contacting your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html) or emailing the State Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/contact-us.html). Be sure to provide your date of birth and address, so that we can verify your registration.

questions.q: If I don't vote in the Primary Election, can I still vote in the General Election?
questions.a: Whether you do or do not vote in a primary election has no bearing on your eligibility to vote in a general election. If you are properly registered, you are eligible to vote.

questions.q: Will my ballot be counted if I don't vote every race on it? What if I leave some races blank?
questions.a: Whether you vote in all races that appear on your ballot, in only some of the races, or in only one race, any vote you cast is always counted. If you prefer not to vote for a candidate or a question, you are entitled to make that choice. It will not affect the counting of your votes in any other races on your ballot.

questions.q: What is the Electoral College and how does it work?
questions.a: See this excellent treatment of the Electoral College (http://www.archives.gov/federal-register/electoral-college/about.html) from the Office of the Federal Register.

questions.q: How does straight party voting work?
questions.a:
When you mark one of the straight party boxes, the machine will record a vote for the candidate from that party in any race where there is a candidate from that party. If you mark the straight party box but also mark the box next to a candidate from a different party lower on the ballot, the individual vote in that race will override the straight party choice in that race only. You will still need to mark non-partisan races such as judicial retention and any ballot questions if you want a vote counted in those races.

questions.q: When are polling places open?
questions.a: On Election Day, polling places are open from 7 AM until 7 PM. In-person absentee voting or "early voting" is also available for all elections. Please refer to our early voting page (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/early-voting.html) for information on dates, times, and locations.

questions.q: Where do I vote?
questions.a:
You can find your polling place, sample ballot and more in the OK Voter Portal (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/).

questions.q: May I write in a candidate's name on my ballot?
questions.a:
No. Generally speaking, write-in voting is not permitted in Oklahoma.

However, military and overseas voters may write in the names of candidates when there is insufficient time for them to vote a normal absentee ballot. This is done on a special, federal write-in absentee ballot. More information is available on the Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP) website (https://www.fvap.gov/oklahoma) or by contacting the State Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/contact-us.html).

Last Modified on Jan 06, 2026

questions.q: I tried to register online to vote, but the Online Voter Registration System says it can't confirm my Driver License. Why?
questions.a:
You must enter your information exactly as it appears on your Driver License/State ID card. (For example, if "northwest" and "street" are abbreviated on your card, do not spell the words out. Use the abbreviated form.)

In addition to your Driver License or State ID, eligible individuals must also have a digital signature on file with Service Oklahoma. (This is the signature that you provided when you applied for, renewed, or updated your Driver License or State ID.)

questions.q: I registered to vote, but I haven't received my Voter ID card. Why?
questions.a:
All Voter Registration Applications regardless of how they are submitted (e.g. online, mail, in person) must be manually processed and approved by the County Election Board Secretary. You are not a registered voter until your Voter Registration Application has been approved.

Once your application has been approved, you will be mailed a Voter ID (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/proof-of-identity.html) card confirming your registration. If your application cannot be approved, you will be mailed a letter from your County Election Board explaining the reason(s) why your application could not be approved and the steps that may be taken to complete the process.

If you do not receive your Voter ID card or a letter within 30 days of submitting your application, please contact your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html) directly.

questions.q: I recently registered to vote, but the OK Voter Portal says it can’t find me. Why?
questions.a:
You are not a registered voter until your Voter Registration Application has been manually processed and approved by the County Election Board Secretary.

If your application was submitted after the voter registration deadline, your application will be processed immediately following the upcoming election.

questions.q: I know I’m registered to vote, but the OK Voter Portal says it can’t find me. Has my voter registration been deleted?
questions.a:
While it is possible that your voter registration may have been removed as part of the voter registration maintenance process required by law, more often than not the problem is the result of a user error.

First - Check your browser. The portal is compatible with the latest versions of Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, and Apple Safari.

Next - Be sure you are entering your information exactly as it appears on your voter registration record.

Finally - Verify that your information is entered in the correct order before clicking "find me." (Last name, first name, then date of birth xx-xx-xxxx.)

questions.q: I use a name that is different from my given name. What should I enter when logging into portal?
questions.a: Use the name that you used when you registered to vote. If you are unsure which name you used when you registered, contact your County Election Board or the State Election Board for assistance or refer to your Voter ID card.

questions.q: My name is misspelled on my Voter ID card. How should I enter my name when logging into the portal?
questions.a: You must enter your name exactly as it appears in the registration system in order to access your information. If you need to correct the spelling on your Voter ID card, please contact your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html) directly.

questions.q: I have a hyphenated name. Should I enter the hyphen when logging into the portal?
questions.a: It depends on how your information was entered at the County Election Board. (Remember, the portal is case sensitive!) Try entering your name, both with the hyphen and without the hyphen.

questions.q: I have verified that I am entering my name correctly, but the portal still says it can't find me. What do I do now?
questions.a:
Contact your County Election Board or the State Election Board to verify that your date of birth matches the information in the voter registration system.

If you have confirmed that your date of birth matches the voter registration system, but you are still having issues, try manually typing a "/" between each number before selecting "Find Me."

In some rare instances, when the voter clicks “Find Me,” the browser may transpose or shift the numbers of the voter’s birthdate. (e.g. 10/13/9891 instead of 01/31/1989) If this is the case, please try a different browser or device.

You must have a date of birth on file to access the OK Voter Portal. If you do not have a date of birth on file, you will need to complete a new Voter Registration Application (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) to update your registration.

questions.q: I logged into the portal, but it says I don’t have a sample ballot. Why not?
questions.a:
If you have an election, the portal will display a sample ballot several weeks prior to the election. If you do not have an election, the portal will not display a sample ballot and a message will appear indicating that you do not have a sample ballot available. Sample ballots are tailored to each voter, so your sample ballot may not necessarily be the same as your friend or relative's ballot.

If you have questions about your eligibility to vote in a particular election, contact your County Election Board and/or refer to "Your Voting Districts" information in the OK Voter Portal.

questions.q: I am an Independent voter, why do I have a nonpartisan sample ballot AND a Democratic Primary sample ballot?
questions.a:
Oklahoma is a closed primary state. However, every two years, all recognized parties may choose to open its primary elections to Independent voters. If a party chooses to open its primaries to Independent voters, the portal will display sample ballots for all elections in which Independents are eligible to vote. Independent voters will be able to view a nonpartisan ballot, as well as a primary ballot for those parties which have chosen to open its primaries to Independents.

Voters should understand that they may not necessarily vote all of the ballots displayed. (The portal is simply displaying all of the possible choices.)

Independent voters will receive a nonpartisan ballot at their voting location or upon request of an absentee ballot, UNLESS they specifically request to receive a primary ballot for a party has that has opened its primaries to Independents.

questions.q: I want to view sample ballots for elections across the state. Can I do that through the portal?
questions.a:
Voters who would like to see sample ballots for other elections may request those sample ballots by contacting the County Election Board or the State Election Board. Sample ballots are also available at your County Election Board office.

Please keep in mind that there are almost two-thousand precincts across the state and hundreds of ballot styles (or combinations) for a typical statewide election. Election officials may ask you to provide more information about the sample ballots you are requesting, such as the precinct number(s).

questions.q: What is the difference between the PDF sample ballot and the HTML sample ballot?
questions.a: The ballots are the same, but they are displayed in a different format. Voters who would like to print a copy of their sample ballot, should select the “PDF” version. The HTML version has accessibility features that are useful to some votes (such as adjustable font size.) The HTML version is also better for users using text-to-speech tools.

questions.q: I am trying to update my registration address in the portal, but it says it doesn’t recognize my new address. Why?
questions.a:
This may be caused by one of several reasons.

1. The portal will only allow voters to update an address, provided they have not moved to a different county.

If you have moved to a new county, you can submit a new Voter Registration Application through the Online Voter Registration System (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) by clicking "Start the Process" at the top of the OK Voter Portal. If you do not have sufficient information to submit an online application, the portal will direct you back to the OK Voter Portal "registration wizard” (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) to complete a new, paper Voter Registration Application. (Be sure to print, sign, and mail or hand deliver the application to your County Election Board to complete the process.)

You can also download an application (https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/elections/forms/voter-registration-application.pdf) from the State Election Board website or pick up an application from your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html). Applications are also available at most tag agencies, libraries, and post offices.

2. The portal cannot recognize an address that is not in the system.

If you have moved into a new construction home or a new housing addition, you may have an address that has not yet been added to the various mapping systems. You will need to complete a new Voter Registration Application (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) and submit it to your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html). You can submit a new application using the Online Voter Registration System (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) or use the OK Voter Portal "wizard" (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) to complete an application, which can be mailed or hand delivered to your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html).

3. You may have entered the address differently than what is displayed in the system.

Please verify your new address to make sure you did not accidentally omit a street direction or enter the wrong street type or zip code.

If you are certain no mistakes have been made, but you are unable to successfully enter your address, please complete a Voter Registration Application (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/) using the Online Voter Registration System (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) or use the OK Voter Portal "wizard" (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) to complete an application, which can be mailed or hand delivered to your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html).

Once the Voter Registration Application has been received, County Election Board officials and staff can use multiple resources to determine the location of your address and add it to the system.

questions.q: I updated my mailing address and received my new Voter ID card, but the card was sent to my residence address. Why?
questions.a:
There are a couple of reasons why this may have happened.

1. State law requires Voter ID cards to be mailed to your residence address, unless you do not have a valid USPS address, as defined by statute. (See 26 O.S. § 4-113. (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=78465))

If you have questions about your Voter ID card or need to confirm your residence address, please contact your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html) directly.

2. Updating your mailing address does not automatically update your residence address.

Since these addresses may be different, you must select to update each address individually. You may use the portal to submit a new address change. Be sure to select one of the following:

- Change my residence address within my current county
- Change my residence address to another county

questions.q: I just changed my party affiliation. Now, I’m trying to change my address and the portal won’t let me. Why?
questions.a: Changes made using the portal must be manually processed. The portal will not allow an additional change until the first one has been processed by the County Election Board. If you have questions about the status of your requests, please contact your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html) directly.

questions.q: I have tried several times to make changes to my registration and I keep getting an error code. What’s causing this to happen?
questions.a:
Error codes are generally triggered by a user error. Wait 10-15 minutes. Refresh your page and enter your information again.

If the error code continues to appear, it is strongly recommended that you submit a new Voter Registration Application using the OK Voter Portal's Online Voter Registration System (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) or submit a paper, Voter Registration Application (https://okvoterportal.okelections.us/Home/RegWizard) by mail or in person to your County Election Board (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/about-us/county-election-boards.html) in order to avoid missing any upcoming deadline.

questions.q: The election is over, but the portal isn't displaying my voter history. Why?
questions.a: The portal is a public-facing information system ONLY. Voter history must be manually entered into the voter registration system by election officials and then updated in the portal. For large, statewide elections this can often take 4-5 weeks or longer.

questions.q: What do the asterisks mean next to the election date in my voter history?
questions.a:
State law prohibits the public disclosure of your "method of voting" (e.g. absentee, in-person absentee, Election Day) for ALL elections, EXCEPT regularly scheduled federal elections, state elections, and statewide question elections. (See 26 O.S. § 7-138 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=78594).)

If you voted in an election that does not allow your "method of voting" to be disclosed, you will see a series of asterisks next to the election date (*********). This indicates that you cast a ballot in that election, but that your "method of voting" may not be publicly disclosed.

questions.q: I didn't vote in the last election, but my voter history has a message that says "Data Entry By County Election Bd Not Yet Complete." Why?
questions.a:
This is a default message. Once your County Election Board has completed entering its voter history data, the message will disappear and the election date will no longer appear in your voter history.

questions.q: How do I become a notary public?
questions.a: The Oklahoma Secretary of State commissions notaries public. Learn more here (https://www.sos.ok.gov/notary/info/gettingStarted.aspx).

questions.q: How do I find a notary public?
questions.a:
The Oklahoma Secretary of State maintains a searchable database of notaries here (https://www.sos.ok.gov/notary/search.aspx).

 What are the general duties of a notary public.

 The Oklahoma Secretary of State commissions notaries public. Learn more here (https://www.sos.ok.gov/notary/info/gettingStarted.aspx).

questions.q: Are absentee ballot affidavits required to be notarized?
questions.a:
For standard absentee ballot affidavits, state law requires an absentee voter’s signature to be notarized. (26 O.S. §14-108 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=438383))

 However, there are alternatives to notarization of absentee ballot affidavits.

There are absentee ballots for certain special conditions, which have alternate methods for executing an absentee ballot affidavit. Learn more here (https://oklahoma.gov/elections/voters/absentee-voting.html).

questions.q: Can a notary public charge a fee to notarize an absentee ballot affidavit?
questions.a: No. Under state law Oklahoma notaries are not allowed to charge a fee to notarize an absentee ballot affidavit. (26 O.S. §14-108 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=438383) and 49 O.S. §5 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/deliverdocument.asp?id=80014&hits=))

questions.q: How does a notary verify the identity of an absentee voter?
questions.a: State law requires a notary to determine the identity of a person “either from personal knowledge or from satisfactory evidence.” (49 O.S. §113 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=80031))

questions.q: Is a notary required to keep a record of the absentee ballot affidavits that are notarized?
questions.a: Yes. State law requires a notary public to maintain a log of all absentee ballot affidavits that he or she notarizes for a period of at least two (2) years after the date of the election. (26 O.S. §14-108.1 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=466286)) Notaries may contact the Secretary of State’s office for recommendations (https://www.sos.ok.gov/notary/info/faqs.aspx) about the information notaries should record and maintain for their official acts. Otherwise, state law does not specify whether a place of business or other entity shall keep and maintain any additional documentation.

questions.q: Are there certain persons who are not allowed to notarize an absentee ballot?
questions.a: Yes. State law prohibits a candidate whose name appears on the ballot, a campaign chairperson, or a campaign treasurer from notarizing an absentee ballot. (26 O.S. §14-108 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=438383))

questions.q: Are there limits on the number of absentee ballots a notary public may notarize?
questions.a:
Yes. State law allows a notary to notarize up to twenty (20) absentee ballot affidavits at a single election. Subject to the exceptions below, this twenty-signature notarization limit applies statewide.

 However, there are exceptions to this limit:

- The limit of twenty (20) affidavits does not apply to the notarization of absentee ballot affidavits at the place of business of a notary public that is open to the general public during the normal business hours.
- A notary public can request permission from a county election board secretary to notarize more than twenty (20) absentee ballots at a single election in the county served by that secretary.

 (See 26 O.S. §14-108.1 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=466286) as amended in May 2020 by Section 8 of SB 1779)

questions.q: Must a notary public possess a waiver for each county that he or she wishes to notarize ballots in?
questions.a: The twenty-signature notarization limit applies statewide. To the extent that a notary public may or will exceed the twenty-signature notarization limit, he or she must have a waiver from the county election board secretary in any county and for any election he or she wishes to notarize absentee ballot affidavits.

questions.q: How long does a notary waiver remain valid?
questions.a: Any waiver to exceed the twenty-signature notarization limit granted by a county election board secretary is valid only for the election(s) a notary public is authorized to exceed the limit.

questions.q: Does a political party headquarters or campaign office qualify for a “place of business” exception to notary's limit on notarizing 20 absentee affidavits for a single election?
questions.a: State law says the limit of 20 affidavits does not apply to the notarization of absentee ballot affidavits “at the place of business of a notary public” that is “open to the general public during the normal business hours.” If the office meets these requirements, the exception applies. If not, it is recommended that a notary public request permission from the county election board secretary to notarize more than 20 absentee ballot affidavits at a single election in that county. (See 26 O.S. §14-108.1 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=466286) as amended in May 2020 by Section 8 of SB 1779)

questions.q: Can “drive-thru” notarization services be offered for absentee ballot affidavits?
questions.a: Neither federal nor state law prohibit this type of service, but participating notaries must meet one of the exceptions previously described to notarize more than twenty (20) absentee ballot affidavits at a single election.

questions.q: Can a notary public request an absentee ballot on behalf of another person, or submit a voted absentee ballot to election officials on behalf of another voter?
questions.a:
No. Except for a few special circumstances, a voter must apply for his or her own absentee ballot, and must return his or her absentee ballot to election officials. State law specifically prohibits a notary public or an agent working on behalf of the notary from doing any of the following (26 O.S. §14-108.1 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=466286)):

- Requesting absentee ballots on behalf of another voter; or
- Assisting another voter in requesting absentee ballots; or
- Receiving by mail an absentee ballot on behalf of another voter; or
- Submitting a completed absentee ballot on behalf of another voter.

questions.q: Can an absentee ballot affidavit be notarized remotely?
questions.a: Yes. An absentee ballot affidavit that is legally notarized by a method allowed under Oklahoma law will be accepted as valid by a county election board. However, an Oklahoma notary cannot charge an absentee voter the fee that is customary for remotely notarizing documents.

questions.q: Can a notary public provide a postage stamp or an envelope to an absentee voter for the purpose of returning an absentee ballot to the county election board?
questions.a:
Yes. A stamp and/or envelope are not considered a “thing of value” for the purposes of voting. (See 26 O.S. §16-106 (https://www.oscn.net/applications/oscn/DeliverDocument.asp?CiteID=78762) as amended in May 2020 by Section 13 of SB 1779)
